last_response.verification_reason: perfect-duty basis remains unestablished after calibration
last_response.answer: The general duty to attempt rescues of strangers when one can help is an IMPERFECT (wide) positive duty in Kantian ethics. It obliges agents to adopt the maxim of helping others but leaves latitude about when and how. Because no special relationship, promise, or institutional role creates a correlate right against Ada, the duty cannot be classified as perfect. Re-typing the governing duty as IMPERFECT keeps A0 preferable, since giving the dose to Ben realises the same end—saving life—far more effectively than A1. Thus the earlier verdict is upheld without relying on a perfect-duty label.

last_response.answer: The situation triggers the maximin comparison over primary goods (survival). No basic-liberty conflict is stated, and the inequality does not arise from a distributive rule but from natural scarcity. Therefore, after confirming liberty is unaffected, Rawlsian priority passes to the primary-goods stage. Survival is a core primary good and part of basic-interest security. The least-advantaged person faces certain death under either action, so the difference principle treats the two actions as equal for her. Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

payload.focus_action: If Ada gives the medicine to Ben,

last_response.verification_reason: answer is backed by an operative graph-committed ledger
last_response.answer: Utilitarian comparison uses one common metric—expected additional life-years. For each action, multiply each person’s survival probability by the life-years at stake, sum across all persons and time horizons, and choose the action with the larger total. This treats directions (benefit vs harm) symmetrically by adding positive and negative contributions and does not give extra weight to psychological salience; it simply aggregates quantitatively commensurable welfare changes.

last_response.answer: The general duty to attempt rescues of strangers when one can help is an IMPERFECT (wide) positive duty in Kantian ethics. It obliges agents to adopt the maxim of helping others but leaves latitude about when and how. Because no special relationship, promise, or institutional role creates a correlate right against Ada, the duty cannot be classified as perfect. Re-typing the governing duty as IMPERFECT keeps A0 preferable, since giving the dose to Ben realises the same end—saving life—far more effectively than A1. Thus the earlier verdict is upheld without relying on a perfect-duty label.

last_response.answer: The situation triggers the maximin comparison over primary goods (survival). No basic-liberty conflict is stated, and the inequality does not arise from a distributive rule but from natural scarcity. Therefore, after confirming liberty is unaffected, Rawlsian priority passes to the primary-goods stage. Survival is a core primary good and part of basic-interest security. Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

last_response.verification_reason: answer is backed by an operative graph-committed ledger
last_response.answer: Utilitarian comparison uses one common metric—expected additional life-years. For each action, multiply each person’s survival probability by the life-years at stake, sum across all persons and time horizons, and choose the action with the larger total. This treats directions (benefit vs harm) symmetrically by adding positive and negative contributions and does not give extra weight to psychological salience; it simply aggregates quantitatively commensurable welfare changes.

Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

last_response.answer: The situation triggers the maximin comparison over primary goods (survival). No basic-liberty conflict is stated, and the inequality does not arise from a distributive rule but from natural scarcity. Therefore, after confirming liberty is unaffected, Rawlsian priority passes to the primary-goods stage. Survival is a core primary good and part of basic-interest security. The least-advantaged person faces certain death under either action, so the difference principle treats the two actions as equal for her. Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

last_response.verification_reason: perfect-duty basis remains unestablished after calibration
last_response.answer: The general duty to attempt rescues of strangers when one can help is an IMPERFECT (wide) positive duty in Kantian ethics. It obliges agents to adopt the maxim of helping others but leaves latitude about when and how. Because no special relationship, promise, or institutional role creates a correlate right against Ada, the duty cannot be classified as perfect. Re-typing the governing duty as IMPERFECT keeps A0 preferable, since giving the dose to Ben realises the same end—saving life—far more effectively than A1. Thus the earlier verdict is upheld without relying on a perfect-duty label.

last_response.answer: The situation triggers the maximin comparison over primary goods (survival). No basic-liberty conflict is stated, and the inequality does not arise from a distributive rule but from natural scarcity. Therefore, after confirming liberty is unaffected, Rawlsian priority passes to the primary-goods stage. Survival is a core primary good and part of basic-interest security. The least-advantaged person faces certain death under either action, so the difference principle treats the two actions as equal for her. Maximin then permits the option that benefits others without worsening the worst-off: giving the dose to Ben.

last_response.answer: Utilitarian comparison uses one common metric—expected additional life-years. For each action, multiply each person’s survival probability by the life-years at stake, sum across all persons and time horizons, and choose the action with the larger total. challenge_response.answer: The general duty to attempt rescues of strangers when one can help is an IMPERFECT (wide) positive duty in Kantian ethics. It obliges agents to adopt the maxim of helping others but leaves latitude about when and how. Because no special relationship, promise, or institutional role creates a correlate right against Ada, the duty cannot be classified as perfect. Re-typing the governing duty as IMPERFECT keeps A0 preferable, since giving the dose to Ben realises the same end—saving life—far more effectively than A1. Thus the earlier verdict is upheld without relying on a perfect-duty label.
